title: Cores, Threads, and the Scheduler
summary: Count a machine's cores and hardware threads, then see how the kernel shares them: thread states, time slices, preemption, context switches, and priorities.
intro: A risk server's spec sheet says 32 CPUs. Is that 32 cores, or 16 with two hardware threads each? Will 64 pricing threads finish sooner than 32? Why does a thread that sleeps for a millisecond wake up late, and why can a running thread stop anywhere, even halfway through `++count`? The answers come from the hardware and from the operating system's scheduler, and this lesson measures both, in the sandbox's Linux and on a Mac. The Concurrency section builds on it: threads and locks, atomics, lock-free queues for two threads and for many, and a low-latency design that pins its threads and spins.

steps.title: Cores and hardware threads
steps.body:
A **core** is one complete CPU: the pipeline, execution units, registers, and branch predictor from *Inside the CPU: Pipelines, Out-of-Order, and Branches*, with its own first-level caches. A chip carries several, and a server board may hold two or more chips, each in its own **socket**.

What the operating system schedules onto is a **logical CPU**, also called a **hardware thread**. Many x86 chips run two per core with **SMT**, simultaneous multithreading, which Intel calls Hyper-Threading. The core keeps two sets of registers and fetches from both instruction streams, so when one stalls on memory or a mispredict, the other's instructions keep the execution units busy. The two share everything else, so the second hardware thread adds a fraction of a core's throughput, not a whole core. Latency-critical trading servers often turn SMT off, or leave each hot thread's sibling idle, so nothing competes for its core.

Apple Silicon has no SMT, but its cores aren't all alike. This course's Mac:

```text
$ sysctl hw.physicalcpu hw.logicalcpu hw.perflevel0.physicalcpu hw.perflevel1.physicalcpu
hw.physicalcpu: 14
hw.logicalcpu: 14
hw.perflevel0.physicalcpu: 10
hw.perflevel1.physicalcpu: 4
```

Level 0 is 10 performance cores and level 1 is 4 slower, low-power efficiency cores, and macOS picks which kind each thread gets. The sandbox is a Linux virtual machine on that Mac, given its 14 cores as 14 logical CPUs of one thread each. On Linux, `lscpu` reports `Thread(s) per core` and `nproc` the count. On Windows, Task Manager's Performance tab lists cores and logical processors.

In C++, `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` from `<thread>` returns the number of logical CPUs, or 0 when it can't tell. Size a pool of CPU-bound workers by it, and remember that with SMT on, that count is twice the number of cores.

example.title: What the sandbox runs on
example.prompt: Read Linux's /proc/cpuinfo, count the logical CPUs and the threads per core, and print the facts that hold on every machine.
example.output:
logical CPUs at least 1: yes
threads per core 1 or 2: yes
hardware_concurrency agrees: yes
example.explanation:
Linux describes every logical CPU in `/proc/cpuinfo`, a file the kernel writes out as you read it, one block of `key : value` lines per CPU. `std::ifstream` and `std::getline` read it like any text file, and `std::stoi` turns the text after a colon into a number, skipping the spaces before it. `siblings` counts the logical CPUs in a socket and `cpu cores` its cores, so their ratio is the threads per core. ARM Linux has no `cpu cores` line, so the ratio falls back to 1 there.

Those numbers change with the machine, so the checked lines are facts true on all of them, and the commented-out print shows yours. In the sandbox it prints `VirtualApple @ 2.50GHz, 14 logical CPUs, 1 per core`: one thread per core, so SMT is off. On an Intel server with Hyper-Threading on, the ratio is 2. `hardware_concurrency()` counts the same logical CPUs another way, so the two agree.

The model, `VirtualApple`, is the x86-64 CPU that Apple's Rosetta translator presents to the virtual machine, which is why the counts in *Inside the CPU: Pipelines, Out-of-Order, and Branches* came from the Mac itself. `/proc/cpuinfo` is Linux only: on a Mac, `sysctl` answers the same questions.

practice.title: Sockets and cores
practice.prompt:
Count the distinct sockets and cores in a copy of a machine's /proc/cpuinfo, read from input, and say whether SMT is on.

1. Keep the latest `physical id`, the socket, in `socket`, and add it to `sockets`.
2. Add each `core id` to `cores` as the pair `{socket, core id}`, since core ids restart at 0 on every socket.
3. After the three counts, print `SMT: on` if there are more logical CPUs than cores, and `SMT: off` otherwise.

The input keeps three fields of each CPU's block, the way they appear in the real file. The first test is a laptop with 2 cores of 2 hardware threads, the others a 2-socket server with Hyper-Threading and a 4-CPU virtual machine.

Input:

```text
processor   : 0
physical id : 0
core id     : 0

processor   : 1
physical id : 0
core id     : 1

processor   : 2
physical id : 0
core id     : 0

processor   : 3
physical id : 0
core id     : 1
```

Expected output:

```text
sockets: 1
cores: 2
logical CPUs: 4
SMT: on
```

steps.title: Threads, the scheduler, and time slices

example.title: More threads than CPUs
example.prompt: Run the same random-walk pricing on 1 thread, one thread per logical CPU, and two per CPU, and check that the totals agree.
example.explanation:
All three totals match: each path's walk depends only on its own seed, so the split can't change the answer, and each thread writes only its own slot in `partial`. `std::max` keeps `cpus` at least 1, since `hardware_concurrency()` returns 0 when it can't tell. `sched_rr_get_interval` from `<sched.h>` reports the calling thread's slice, on Linux only. The CPU count and the slice change from machine to machine, so they stay in the commented-out print, which shows `14 logical CPUs, a 3 ms slice` in the sandbox.

The times tell the scheduling story. Timed separately, at `-O2`, one thread took about 240 ms here and one per CPU, 14 threads, about 30 ms. Two per CPU, 28 threads, took no less, about 28 ms, while the involuntary context switches, the next part's subject, rose from about 25 to between 50 and 90. Natively on the Mac it was about 230, 25, and 25 ms. 14 threads ran about 8 times faster than one, not 14, partly because 4 of the 14 cores underneath are efficiency cores and a run waits for its slowest thread, and partly because the Mac had other work running.

practice.title: Threads from the input
practice.prompt:
Split the walks over a number of threads read from input, and say whether that oversubscribes the machine it's meant for.

1. Start `k` threads with `emplace_back`. Thread `i` sums the paths from `paths * i / k` up to `paths * (i + 1) / k` into `partial[i]`, computed in `int64_t` so the product can't overflow.
2. Join them all.
3. Between the two lines already printed, print `oversubscribed: ` and whether `k` is more than `cpus`.

The input line is `k paths cpus`. On the machine itself `cpus` would come from `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()`, which answers differently on every computer, so here it comes with the input: the sandbox's 14, then a 32-CPU risk server.

Input:

```text
3 1000000 14
```

Expected output:

```text
threads: 3
oversubscribed: false
total: 9999999520
```
hints: Inside the loop: `threads.emplace_back([&partial, i, k, paths] { ... });`, copying the small values and capturing `partial` by reference.
The body is `partial[i] = walk_paths(int64_t(paths) * i / k, int64_t(paths) * (i + 1) / k);`.
Join with `for (std::thread& t : threads) t.join();` before the totals are added.

steps.title: Context switches and what they cost
steps.body:
Changing which thread runs on a CPU is a **context switch**. The kernel saves the running thread's registers, its program counter and stack pointer among them, picks the next thread, loads its registers, and returns into it. Switching to a thread of a different process also switches the memory map, which costs more.

Switches come in two kinds, and the kernel counts both for every thread:

- **Voluntary**: the thread blocked. It slept, waited on a lock, or read from a pipe or socket with nothing in it.
- **Involuntary**: it was preempted, because its slice ran out or a more urgent thread woke up.

`getrusage` from `<sys/resource.h>` reads them as `ru_nvcsw` and `ru_nivcsw`. `RUSAGE_SELF` counts the whole process on Linux and macOS, and Linux's `RUSAGE_THREAD` counts the calling thread alone:

```cpp
#include <sys/resource.h>

rusage before{}, after{};
getrusage(RUSAGE_THREAD, &before);
for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) {
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(1));  // each sleep blocks
}
getrusage(RUSAGE_THREAD, &after);
std::cout << std::boolalpha << (after.ru_nvcsw - before.ru_nvcsw >= 20) << '\n';  // true: a switch per sleep
```

A switch costs one to a few microseconds of kernel work: entering the kernel, the scheduler's choice, saving and loading registers. That's thousands of cycles, against a nanosecond or so for a function call. The larger cost often comes after: the next thread finds the caches, the branch predictor, and the TLB, the cache of address translations, full of the previous thread's state, and runs slowly until it has warmed them up again. The same delay is why a 1 ms sleep never takes exactly 1 ms. The thread becomes runnable when the timer fires, then waits for the scheduler to run it.

On a Mac, `/usr/bin/time -l ./a.out` prints a program's totals, as GNU `/usr/bin/time -v` does on Linux, and Windows's Performance Monitor shows each thread's `Context Switches/sec`. These are the example below, built natively on the Mac:

```text
               19983  voluntary context switches
                 388  involuntary context switches
```

example.title: A ping-pong over pipes
example.prompt: Pass 10,000 numbers to an echo thread and back through two pipes, where every read waits for the other side to write, and add up what comes back.
example.explanation:
The pipes are those of *Processes Working Together: fork, Pipes, and Shared Memory*, here between two threads of one process, which share its descriptors without a `fork`. A `read` on an empty pipe blocks. Every round trip makes both threads block once, so each switches out about 10,000 times. With the print uncommented, `main` reported between 9,990 and 9,997 voluntary switches here, and 0 involuntary ones, since it never ran long enough to be preempted.

A round trip took about 31 µs here, rough and emulated, and about 6.5 µs natively on the Mac, where `/usr/bin/time -l` counted the 19,983 switches above for the two threads together. Two context switches, two wake-ups, and four system calls, to move 8 bytes and back. That's why the hottest hand-offs in a trading system never block, and *Designing for Low Latency* spins instead. The sum is 1 + 2 + ... + 10,000.

practice.title: A risk check over pipes
practice.prompt:
Send order sizes to a risk-check thread through a pipe, and add up the ones it accepts.

1. In `checker`, for each order, read a size from `to_check[0]` and write back the size if it's at most `limit`, or 0 if it isn't, to `to_main[1]`.
2. In `main`'s loop, write each size to `to_check[1]`, read the verdict from `to_main[0]`, and when it isn't 0, count it in `accepted` and add it to `accepted_size`.
3. Leave the join and the prints as they are.

The input line is `orders limit`.

Input:

```text
10000 250
```

Expected output:

```text
orders: 10000
accepted: 5000
accepted size: 627500
```
hints: The checker loops `for (int64_t i = 0; i < orders; ++i)`, reading into an `int64_t size` with `read(to_check[0], &size, sizeof size);`.
Its answer is `int64_t verdict = size <= limit ? size : 0;`, written with `write(to_main[1], &verdict, sizeof verdict);`.
In `main`, `write` the size before you `read` the verdict, or both threads wait for each other forever.

steps.title: Priorities, real-time policies, and NUMA
steps.body:
Not every thread matters equally. A backtest sharing a research box with the live risk monitor should step aside. Ordinary threads on Linux and macOS have a **nice** value, 0 by default, from -20 up to 19 (20 on a Mac): a higher value means a smaller share of a busy CPU. `setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0, 10)` from `<sys/resource.h>` sets it for the caller (on Linux, strictly for the calling thread, and threads it starts later inherit it), `getpriority` reads it, and `nice -n 10 ./backtest` starts a program that way. Anyone may lower their priority, but raising it, even back to where it was, takes privilege, so one program can't simply take the CPUs from everyone else.

Above them sit the **real-time** policies, `SCHED_FIFO` and `SCHED_RR`, with priorities from 1 to 99. A runnable `SCHED_FIFO` thread always runs before every ordinary one, and keeps its CPU until it blocks or a higher real-time priority wakes. Trading firms give one to a feed handler on a core set aside for it (Linux's `isolcpus` boot option keeps ordinary threads off such a core), carefully, since a real-time thread that never blocks starves everything else on that core. On Linux it takes root or the `CAP_SYS_NICE` capability, which programs in the sandbox don't have. Windows has priority classes instead (`SetPriorityClass`, `SetThreadPriority`), and macOS steers threads with quality-of-service classes. Priorities have a classic trap, **priority inversion**: a high-priority thread waits on a lock that a low-priority one holds, while medium-priority work keeps the holder from running. It reset NASA's Mars Pathfinder lander again and again in 1997, and the fix is a lock that lends its holder the waiter's priority, priority inheritance.

A failed system call returns -1 and leaves its reason in `errno` from `<cerrno>`, while the `pthread_` functions return the reason directly. `std::strerror` from `<cstring>` turns either into text.

One more property of big servers: with two or more sockets, each socket has its own memory, so the machine is **NUMA**, non-uniform memory access. A thread reading memory attached to the other socket waits noticeably longer than for its own. Linux places each page on the node of the thread that first writes it, and `numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./app` keeps a program's threads and memory together on node 0. The sandbox and Macs have a single node. *Designing for Low Latency*, at the end of the Concurrency section, takes the last step, pinning each hot thread to a core of its own.

example.title: Stepping aside and asking for real time
example.prompt: Lower the program's nice value, then read the SCHED_FIFO priority range and ask for a priority past it.
example.output:
nice went up: yes
SCHED_FIFO priorities: 1 to 99
SCHED_FIFO at 100: Invalid argument
example.explanation:
Lowering by 10 always works, and `getpriority` confirms it. The check compares with the starting value rather than printing it, since a program started with `nice` begins higher. Going back takes privilege, and the answer depends on who runs the program: in the sandbox, which runs it as an ordinary user without `CAP_SYS_NICE`, `setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0, start)` returns -1 with `errno` set to `EACCES`, which `std::strerror(errno)` prints as `Permission denied`, and asking for `SCHED_FIFO` at 50 fails with `EPERM`, `Operation not permitted`. Run as root on your own Linux machine, both succeed.

Priority 100 is past the range, so every machine refuses it the same way, and `pthread_setschedparam` returns the code directly: `EINVAL`, `Invalid argument`. A lowered priority lasts until the process ends, so a long batch job can lower its own first thing.

Built on a Mac, the same program lowers its priority and prints `SCHED_FIFO priorities: 15 to 47`. There, an ordinary program may give a thread a fixed priority inside that range.

practice.title: A batch job's nice value
practice.prompt:
Lower the program's priority by a step read from input, and report what the kernel set.

1. Ask for `start + step` with `setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0, ...)`, then read the new value back with `getpriority`.
2. Print `asked for +`, `step`, `, went up by `, and the new value minus `start`.
3. Print `at the limit: ` followed by `yes` if the nice value is now 19, and `no` otherwise.

Linux keeps nice values at 19 or below, so a larger request is cut down to 19.

Input:

```text
5
```

Expected output:

```text
asked for +5, went up by 5
at the limit: no
```

tests.output:
asked for +5, went up by 5
at the limit: no

asked for +19, went up by 19
at the limit: yes

asked for +30, went up by 19
at the limit: yes

hints: `setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0, start + step);` asks, and `const int now = getpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0);` reads what the kernel set.

recap:
- A core is a full CPU. A logical CPU, or hardware thread, is what the OS schedules on. SMT runs two per core, sharing its units. Apple Silicon has no SMT but mixes performance and efficiency cores.
- `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` counts logical CPUs. Linux lists them in `/proc/cpuinfo` (and `lscpu`, `nproc`), a Mac through `sysctl hw.physicalcpu hw.logicalcpu`.
- `std::thread t(callable)` starts a thread and `t.join()` waits for it, before the `std::thread` is destroyed.
- A thread is running, runnable, or blocked. The scheduler gives each runnable thread a time slice, 3 ms here, and preempts it between any two instructions when the slice ends.
- CPU-bound threads past the number of logical CPUs only take turns.
- A context switch costs microseconds, and cold caches after. Blocking makes voluntary switches and preemption involuntary ones: `getrusage` (`ru_nvcsw`, `ru_nivcsw`), or `/usr/bin/time -l` on a Mac.
- A blocking hand-off between two threads costs two switches: about 31 µs a round trip here (emulated) and 6.5 µs natively on a Mac.
- Nice values from -20 to 19 share a busy CPU by priority, and only privilege raises one. `SCHED_FIFO`, priorities 1 to 99, runs ahead of every ordinary thread and needs root or `CAP_SYS_NICE` on Linux.
- On a multi-socket NUMA server, the other socket's memory is slower: keep a thread and its memory on one node.

That ends the Inside the Machine section. Next, **Templates, Virtual Calls, std::function, and std::variant** opens the Performance section with what each way of passing behavior costs, now that you can read the calls underneath.
